Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is much more characteristic of sexual trauma than a mugging/robbery. In a robbery case it is not impossible, but without any corroborating interpersonal violation, bodily disgust, or related threat/memory content, this item is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: Emotional closeness as a trigger is difficult to link to the stated trauma type of mugging/robbery and to the rest of the profile. The other triggers, threat items, and memory content point to danger/safety and coercion themes, whereas this item implies an intimacy/interpersonal-betrayal theme that is not represented elsewhere.

vignette: Priya, a 22-year-old South Asian woman and delivery driver, experienced a traumatic event that has left her grappling with PTSD. About six months ago, she was mugged on one of her delivery routes. The assailant forced her to hand over her belongings and, in the process, threatened her repeatedly. Since then, Priya’s life has been marked by intense fear and avoidance. Priya had come to believe that the loss of autonomy during the robbery was particularly traumatic; she felt helpless and isolated as if no one could protect her. This sense of helplessness and isolation led her to use drugs and engage in magical thinking—telling herself that the event did not really happen or was not that bad—to cope with the intense feelings of guilt over her perceived lack of action during the incident. These beliefs have also made her hyper-vigilant, always planning escape routes wherever she goes. She wakes frequently at night to check if she is safe and finds it nearly impossible to relax even when she knows she is in a secure environment. Priya’s traumatic experience has left her with fragmented memories of the event; sometimes, she experiences emotional intensity without clear visual recollections, while other times she hears voices from that terrifying day in her mind. The memory fragments often trigger her sense of threat and reinforce her negative appraisals. For instance, the auditory recall of the assailant’s voice makes her feel as though danger is imminent, which heightens her vigilance and further isolates her from others. She avoids driving because it reminds her of the moment she was robbed, triggering her belief that she cannot protect herself. Priya’s intense reactions to triggers have also led her to use drugs more frequently, a behavior she has come to rely on to numb the overwhelming feelings of guilt and helplessness. This avoidance extends beyond her personal life; she now takes longer routes or avoids certain areas while driving for work, which has impacted her job performance. Her supervisor has noticed changes in her delivery times, and this stress further exacerbates her negative beliefs about her inability to handle bad situations. Priya’s isolation is palpable; she keeps a distance from people at work and even among friends because she fears they might judge her for not reacting differently during the robbery. The combination of these factors creates a self-reinforcing cycle where each trigger, memory, threat response, and maladaptive strategy feeds into one another. Recently, Priya realized that she could no longer cope with the mounting stress and isolation. She was certain that the only way to break this pattern was by seeking help. Her most significant fear is that she will never be able to trust others or feel safe again, but she hopes that therapy can help her regain a sense of control and peace in her life. The cumulative impact of these experiences has left Priya feeling both trapped and isolated, desperately searching for ways to reclaim her autonomy and security.
